understand_first: Marine insurance is a promise to pay for something that has not happened yet, made by an underwriter who cannot inspect the ship, about a voyage he will never see, to an assured who knows far more than he does. Every principle in this answer is a repair to one specific weakness in that arrangement. Insurable interest stops it being a bet on a stranger's misfortune. Utmost good faith corrects the information imbalance. Indemnity, subrogation and contribution between them ensure the assured is restored exactly once. Proximate cause confines the insurer to the risk he agreed to run. And mitigation stops the assured from becoming careless because someone else is paying. Learn them as answers to problems rather than as a list, and the examples write themselves.

blocks.h: 1. The statute these principles come from

blocks.p: For an Indian examination the governing statute is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963. It codifies the law of marine insurance in India and follows the English Marine Insurance Act 1906 closely - the 1906 Act may be named as the source it follows, but it must not be cited in its place, and the later English reforms of insurance law do not apply in India. Section 3 gives the contract itself: a contract of marine insurance is an agreement whereby the insurer undertakes to indemnify the assured, in the manner and to the extent thereby agreed, against marine losses.

The principles below are not decoration. Marine insurance is a promise to pay for something that has not happened yet, made by someone who cannot inspect the ship, about a voyage he cannot watch. Each principle answers one way that arrangement could be abused.

The rule. Section 7 - every person has an insurable interest who is interested in a marine adventure; in particular, a person is so interested where he stands in any legal or equitable relation to the adventure or to any insurable property at risk, such that he may benefit by its safety or due arrival, may be prejudiced by its loss or damage or detention, or may incur liability in respect of it. Section 8 fixes the timing: the assured must be interested at the time of the loss, though he need not be when the insurance is effected - and where the subject-matter is insured "lost or not lost" he may recover even if he acquired his interest after the loss, unless he knew of the loss and the insurer did not. Section 6 supplies the sanction: a contract of marine insurance by way of wagering is void, including a policy made "interest or no interest".

Example. A shipowner has an insurable interest in his ship, and a cargo owner in his cargo. A charterer has an interest in the hire he stands to lose and in liabilities he may incur. But a Chief Engineer has no insurable interest in the ship he serves on - he is prejudiced by her loss only in employment, not in property - so a policy he took out on her hull would be a wager and void under section 6. Conversely, if cargo is sold afloat and the risk passes to the buyer, the buyer acquires the interest and can recover, even for a loss that occurred before he bought, under a "lost or not lost" policy.

The rule. Section 19 - a contract of marine insurance is a contract based upon the utmost good faith, and if it is not observed by either party the other may avoid the contract. It is mutual, and it operates before the contract is concluded. Section 20 - the assured must disclose to the insurer, before the contract is concluded, every material circumstance known to him, and he is deemed to know every circumstance which in the ordinary course of business ought to be known by him. A circumstance is material if it would influence the judgement of a prudent insurer in fixing the premium or determining whether to take the risk. In the absence of enquiry, need not be disclosed: circumstances diminishing the risk; matters known or presumed known to the insurer; matters he has waived; and matters covered by an express or implied warranty. Sections 21 and 22 extend the duty to the assured's agent and to representations during negotiation.

Example. The vessel is fixed to load in a port where she has already suffered heavy weather damage to her hatch covers, or the owner knows the main engine has an unrepaired crankshaft defect. Both are material and must be disclosed. Failing to do so entitles the insurer to avoid the policy from the outset - and note the consequence, because it is what makes the principle bite: the contract is voidable, not void, the avoidance operates ab initio, and non-disclosure need not be fraudulent. An honest oversight has the same effect as concealment.

The rule. From section 3 - the insurer undertakes to indemnify. The assured is to be placed, so far as money can, in the position he occupied immediately before the loss - and no better. Marine insurance is a contract of indemnity and not one of profit. Two sections show it working: section 81, where the assured is insured for less than the insurable value, he is deemed his own insurer for the balance; and the measure-of-indemnity provisions, which fix what is actually recoverable rather than what was lost emotionally.

Example. A twenty-year-old auxiliary engine is destroyed by an insured peril and replaced with a new one. The assured recovers the value of what he lost, not the price of a new machine - the betterment is his. Similarly, a ship insured for one crore whose insurable value is two crore recovers only half of a partial loss, because under section 81 she is self-insured for the other half. Marine insurance is a qualified indemnity in practice, because a valued policy agrees the value in advance and that agreed value is conclusive between the parties - which is worth saying, as it is the one place where the principle is deliberately relaxed.

The rule. Section 79 - where the insurer pays for a total loss of the whole, or of an apportionable part of goods, he becomes entitled to take over the interest of the assured in whatever remains of the subject-matter paid for, and is subrogated to all the rights and remedies of the assured in respect of it as from the time of the casualty causing the loss. Where he pays for a partial loss he acquires no title to the subject-matter but is still subrogated to the assured's rights and remedies. Subrogation is the corollary of indemnity: it stops the assured recovering twice for one loss, once from the insurer and once from the wrongdoer.

Example. The ship is damaged in a collision for which the other vessel is wholly to blame. The hull underwriters pay the repair cost, and step into the owner's shoes to pursue the other vessel's owners for that sum - in the owner's name. It follows that the assured must not prejudice those rights: signing away a claim against a stevedore who damaged the cargo, or a repairer who caused the failure, may cost the assured the indemnity itself.

The rule. Section 80 - where the assured is over-insured by double insurance, each insurer is bound, as between himself and the others, to contribute rateably to the loss in proportion to the amount for which he is liable under his own contract; and an insurer who pays more than his proportion may sue the others for contribution, with the remedies of a surety who has overpaid. Contribution is again the servant of indemnity - the assured may claim in full from one insurer, but he cannot collect the same loss twice, and the insurers settle the sharing among themselves.

Example. A cargo is insured by the seller under an open cover and again by the buyer under his own policy, both policies attaching to the same interest for the same voyage. On a claim the assured need not chase both; he recovers from one, and that insurer recovers a rateable proportion from the other under section 80. If the two policies total more than the insurable value, the assured still recovers only the value of the loss.

The rule. Section 55 - the insurer is liable for any loss proximately caused by a peril insured against, and is not liable for any loss which is not so proximately caused. Proximate means the dominant or effective cause, not the one nearest in time. Section 55 then names exclusions which stand unless the policy provides otherwise, and two are worth carrying: the insurer is not liable for loss attributable to the wilful misconduct of the assured, but is liable for a loss proximately caused by an insured peril even though it would not have happened but for the misconduct or negligence of the master or crew.

Example. A ship strands because the officer of the watch made a navigational error. The proximate cause is stranding, an insured peril, and the negligence of the crew does not defeat the claim - section 55 says so expressly. But if the owner himself sent her to sea knowing she was unfit and she is lost in consequence, the dominant cause is his own conduct and the claim fails. That second half is where this principle meets seaworthiness, and it is the reason the two topics are so often examined together.

blocks.h: 8. Mitigation - the duty to sue and labour

blocks.p: The rule. Insurance does not licence the assured to stand and watch. Where the policy contains a suing and labouring clause, section 78 makes the engagement supplementary to the contract of insurance, and the assured may recover from the insurer the expenses properly incurred under it - notwithstanding that the insurer may have paid for a total loss, or that the subject-matter was warranted free from particular average. The assured and his agents are expected to take reasonable measures to avert or minimise a loss.

Example. After a flooding in the engine room, the Chief Engineer runs the emergency bilge suction, arranges shore pumps and lands the damaged spares for cleaning and preservation. Those costs are recoverable as sue and labour, in addition to the claim itself. Doing nothing, and allowing salt water to write off machinery that could have been saved, risks the insurer declining that part of the loss.

The command is discuss, then explain each of the principle with suitable examples. Two things follow. First, every principle must carry an example - a list of principles without examples answers only half the question, and it is the half worth fewer marks because the examples are what show understanding. Second, the number of principles is left to the candidate, so choose a defensible set and head each one. Six is the classical set - insurable interest, utmost good faith, indemnity, subrogation, contribution, proximate cause. Mitigation is a legitimate seventh and is worth adding because it is the one an engineer can speak about from experience. Do not exceed that: a thin list of nine beats nothing.

blocks.h: Anchor every principle to a section

blocks.p: This is what separates a Class I answer from a general-knowledge one. Every principle here has a section of the Marine Insurance Act 1963 behind it - 7 and 8, 19 and 20, 3 and 81, 79, 80, 55, 78 - and quoting the section costs one line and gains disproportionately. Equally important is which Act: for an Indian paper it is the 1963 Act. The English Marine Insurance Act 1906 is the model it follows and may be named as such; citing the 1906 Act instead is a jurisdiction error, and citing later English insurance-law reform is worse, because that reform does not apply in India at all.

blocks.h: The idea that ties them together

blocks.p: Five of the seven exist to enforce one idea: insurance restores, it does not enrich. Indemnity states it. Insurable interest ensures there is a real loss to restore, and not a bet. Subrogation stops the assured recovering the same loss twice, from insurer and wrongdoer. Contribution stops him recovering it twice from two insurers. Mitigation stops him letting the loss grow because someone else is paying. The remaining two protect the bargain itself: utmost good faith ensures the insurer priced the risk he actually took, and proximate cause ensures he pays only for the risk he agreed to carry. Say that in two sentences before the list, and the seven headings stop reading as memorised vocabulary.

ul: Citing the English MIA 1906 for an Indian paper. The 1963 Act governs. Name 1906 only as the model.
Listing the principles and omitting the examples. The stem asks for examples expressly.
Saying insurable interest must exist when the policy is taken out. Section 8 requires it at the time of the loss; it need not exist at inception.
Saying non-disclosure makes the contract void. It is voidable at the insurer's option, avoided ab initio.
Saying the non-disclosure must be fraudulent. It need not be - an innocent failure to disclose a material circumstance is enough.
Treating proximate cause as the last or nearest in time cause. It is the dominant and effective cause.

Saying crew negligence defeats a claim. Section 55 says the opposite - the insurer is liable for a loss proximately caused by an insured peril even though it would not have happened but for the negligence of master or crew.
Confusing subrogation (insurer recovers from the wrongdoer) with contribution (insurer recovers a share from another insurer).
Omitting the effect of under-insurance under section 81 - the assured is his own insurer for the balance.

blocks.p: "You are Chief Engineer. Can you insure the ship?" No - no insurable interest in the hull, so the policy would be a wager and void under section 6. You can insure your own effects and your liability. "Cargo was already lost when the buyer bought it. Can he claim?" Under a "lost or not lost" policy, yes - unless he knew of the loss and the insurer did not (section 8). "The Second Engineer's error caused the flooding. Does the claim fail?" No - section 55(2)(a) preserves the claim for a loss proximately caused by an insured peril notwithstanding the negligence of master or crew. "The owner knew she was unseaworthy and sent her anyway." Different answer - that is the assured's own conduct, and it defeats the claim. "The engine was twenty years old and you got a new one." You recover the value lost, not the betterment - indemnity, not profit.

ul: Which Act governs marine insurance in India? The Marine Insurance Act, 1963.
Define insurable interest. Section 7 - a legal or equitable relation to the adventure or the property at risk, such that you benefit by its safety or are prejudiced by its loss.
When must the interest exist? At the time of the loss - section 8.
What is uberrimae fidei? Section 19 - utmost good faith, mutual, and breach lets the other party avoid the contract.
What need not be disclosed? Section 20 - circumstances diminishing the risk, matters known or presumed known to the insurer, matters waived, and matters covered by a warranty.
What is subrogation? Section 79 - on payment the insurer takes over the assured's rights and remedies against third parties.
What is contribution? Section 80 - rateable sharing between insurers where the assured is over-insured by double insurance.
State the rule of proximate cause. Section 55 - the insurer is liable for loss proximately caused by an insured peril and not otherwise.
What is sue and labour? Section 78 - expenses properly incurred to avert or minimise a loss are recoverable in addition, even if a total loss is paid.

blocks.p: I - U - I - S - C - P - M. Insurable interest (2), Utmost good faith (3), Indemnity (4), Subrogation (5), Contribution (6), Proximate cause (7), Mitigation (8). Sections in the same order: 7 and 8, 19 and 20, 3 and 81, 79, 80, 55, 78. Five of the seven serve indemnity; two protect the bargain.

Section 6 - avoidance of wagering contracts; 'interest or no interest' policies void.
Sections 7 and 8 - insurable interest defined; when interest must attach; 'lost or not lost'.

blocks.p: Jurisdiction is the live risk on this question, not currency. The principles of marine insurance are stable and have not moved; what moves is which statute a candidate cites. For an Indian paper the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 is the operative statute and every section above is a section of it, read in the Act's own text. The English Marine Insurance Act 1906 is the model and may be named as such. Later English reform of insurance law - which changed the consequences of non-disclosure in England - does not apply in India, and the section 19 and 20 position stated above is the Indian one.

Provenance of the text. The Act's sections were read in a full text of the 1963 Act, and the copy used was checked against sections this corpus had already verified independently through earlier papers - sections 2, 19, 20 and 66 - before the unverified sections were relied on. MIW holds no certified consolidated print, so no claim is made about the amendment history of any individual section.

What is not asserted. No case law is cited. The principles are stated from the statute, and the illustrative examples are worked applications of the sections rather than reports of decided cases - no example above should be read as a case authority. Market practice on valued policies, deductibles and Institute Clauses is named where it qualifies a statutory rule but is not detailed, because the stem asks for the principles and the clauses are not part of the Act.

blocks.h: The one connection worth making on this paper

blocks.p: Read this against Q8 on this paper. Section 55 of the Marine Insurance Act preserves a claim despite the negligence of master or crew, but not despite the assured's own conduct - and unseaworthiness is the classic instance of that conduct. Q8 asks what an unseaworthy ship is under the Merchant Shipping Act, which is a criminal question; here the same fact pattern is a recovery question. One ship, one defect, two entirely different consequences depending on which statute is asking. That contrast is worth carrying into the exam, because examiners set the pair deliberately.

retrieval_cards.why: The four exceptions are a standing question and are easily half-remembered.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does non-disclosure make the policy void, and must it be fraudulent?
retrieval_cards.answer: Neither. Under section 19 the innocent party may avoid the contract, so it is voidable at the insurer's option rather than void, and the avoidance operates ab initio. The non-disclosure need not be fraudulent - an honest failure to disclose a material circumstance is enough to found avoidance.
retrieval_cards.why: Two precise points that candidates routinely get the wrong way round.

retrieval_cards.answer: Subrogation, section 79, is the insurer stepping into the assured's shoes to pursue a third party who caused the loss, after paying the claim. Contribution, section 80, is between insurers - where the assured is over-insured by double insurance, each contributes rateably in proportion to his own liability, and an insurer who pays more than his share may sue the others. Both exist to stop the assured recovering the same loss twice.
retrieval_cards.why: The pair is examined together precisely because they are confused.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does the crew's negligence defeat a hull claim?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Section 55(2)(a) provides that the insurer is not liable for loss attributable to the wilful misconduct of the assured, but, unless the policy otherwise provides, he is liable for any loss proximately caused by a peril insured against even though the loss would not have happened but for the misconduct or negligence of the master or crew. The assured's own conduct is a different matter and does defeat the claim.
retrieval_cards.why: The section says the opposite of what candidates assume.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the rule of proximate cause and what 'proximate' means.
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 55(1). Subject to the Act and unless the policy otherwise provides, the insurer is liable for any loss proximately caused by a peril insured against, and is not liable for any loss which is not proximately caused by a peril insured against. Proximate means the dominant and effective cause of the loss, not the cause nearest in time.
retrieval_cards.why: The time-based misreading is the classic error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is sue and labour, and can you recover it on top of a total loss?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 78. Where the policy contains a suing and labouring clause, the engagement is supplementary to the contract of insurance and the assured may recover from the insurer expenses properly incurred under it - notwithstanding that the insurer may have paid for a total loss, or that the subject-matter was warranted free from particular average. So yes, it is recoverable in addition.
retrieval_cards.why: The 'notwithstanding a total loss' point is the part worth the mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the effect of under-insurance?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 81. Where the assured is insured for less than the insurable value, or in the case of a valued policy for less than the policy valuation, he is deemed to be his own insurer in respect of the uninsured balance, and bears that proportion of any loss himself.
retrieval_cards.why: The practical face of indemnity, and the arithmetic examiners like to set.
